A specification of how wallets reach Mailbox Servers, and optionally each other, over one anonymity network.

This ZIP specifies an off-chain channel between Zcash wallets. A wallet that holds another wallet’s Unified Address deposits an encrypted Envelope in a Mailbox, reaching the Mailbox Server over an anonymity network, and the recipient fetches it later. Neither wallet reveals its network identity to the other or to the server.

Nothing is added to the Unified Address. The Mailbox ID and Mailbox Server are derived from the address’s Orchard Receiver, the Envelope is encrypted to that Receiver using the Orchard key agreement, and fetching requires the incoming viewing key. Every first Envelope also starts a Conversation, whose mailboxes rotate each epoch, so that an ongoing exchange does not accumulate metadata under one identifier. Routing is separate from storage: mailboxes are reached over any supported anonymity network, and prompt replies can also go directly between the wallets. Payload types are defined for acknowledgements, text, ZIP 321 payment requests, and PCZTs.

Anyone who holds the recipient’s Orchard incoming viewing key can read and fetch its Envelopes, and a Mailbox Server sees the volume and timing of what each Mailbox ID receives. Appendix A sketches Routing Bindings for the Nym mixnet
Several wallet protocols need a direct channel between wallets, and each wallet that wants one currently builds its own:
Multisig and hardware-signer flows pass PCZTs

On-chain memos are the only standard channel today. Even without their size cap (ZIP 231
) they cost fees, are stored forever, and need a block confirmation per round. ZIP 324

Out-of-band delivery over a mixnet, with a mailbox for offline recipients, has been proposed before.
routes chain-sync and transaction submission through the mixnet, not wallet-to-wallet messages.

Whoever holds an account’s Orchard incoming viewing key can read and fetch every Envelope ever sent to its addresses, and by fetching can cause the server to delete them. It can also derive the secret of every Conversation started with those addresses, and so read, fetch, and send Envelopes in them, in both directions. There is no forward secrecy. Envelopes can reveal more than notes do: a PCZT shows a transaction before it is signed. The viewing keys of the wallet that starts a Conversation give no access to it.

All diversified addresses of an account share one incoming viewing key, so using a different address does not help. Viewing keys of different accounts are unrelated: a user who shares an account’s viewing key, for example with an auditor or a watch-only service, keeps messages from its holder only by receiving them at addresses of another account.

A server never learns a network identity. It sees each Mailbox ID it holds and the number, size, and timing of the Envelopes deposited in and fetched from it. A Contact Mailbox lives as long as its address, and anyone who knows the address can compute its ID and server, so that server holds a long-lived traffic record for the address. Pairwise Mailbox IDs change every epoch and can be computed only by the two wallets and the responder’s viewing key holders.
Diversified addresses of one wallet have unrelated Contact Mailboxes. A server can still link them if the wallet fetches them together, which is why fetches use separate sessions and schedules.
Every address with an Orchard Receiver has a Contact Mailbox whether or not its wallet implements this ZIP, so a sender cannot tell whether its Envelope will be read.

Envelopes do not authenticate their sender. An answer shows the sender that the recipient was online. Both wallets can fetch from the Pairwise Mailboxes of both directions, so each can see when the other’s fetches cause its Envelopes to be deleted, and a wallet in Conversations with two addresses can compare them.
Privacy is bounded by the anonymity set of the Routing Binding. A wallet’s entry point to the network sees its IP address but no Mailbox ID, server, or Zcash address.
Anyone can deposit under any Mailbox ID, at the expense of the server’s storage and the recipient’s bandwidth.
A sender holding only a recipient’s Unified Address can deliver a message with no prior contact, while the recipient is offline.
Unified Addresses and ZIP 316 are unchanged, and first contact needs no key material beyond the recipient’s existing Orchard keys.
A wallet can use many diversified addresses without a Mailbox Server, a network observer, or a sender being able to link them.
No Mailbox Server or network observer learns the network identity of a sender or recipient, and neither wallet learns the other’s.
No party that sees a wallet’s IP address is bound to that wallet’s addresses or mailboxes.
Two wallets can keep exchanging messages without a Mailbox Server accumulating metadata under a long-lived identifier.
An Envelope reveals nothing about its content beyond its size.
The protocol does not depend on any one network or token.
Sender authentication, guaranteed delivery, forward secrecy, and group messaging.
Backup and recovery. Contact Mailboxes can be recomputed from the wallet’s addresses and viewing keys; Conversations cannot.

A Routing Binding carries requests to Mailbox Servers and responses back. It MUST:
hide the wallet’s network identity from the server and from everyone but the wallet’s own entry point to the network;
keep requests and responses confidential and authentic between the wallet and the server;
such that neither the server nor a network observer can tell whether two requests in different sessions come from one wallet.
Its specification states the server address format, the framing of requests, responses, and Envelopes sent in fast mode, what a session is, and what each party can observe.
A wallet MUST use a new session for each Deposit, and MUST NOT use one session for two Mailbox IDs. It MUST NOT bypass the anonymity network when it is unavailable.
A Routing Binding MAY define addresses at which a wallet can receive Envelopes directly for a limited time without revealing its network identity to the sender.

Wallets SHOULD NOT fetch the Contact Mailboxes of an account whose incoming viewing key they have exported, and SHOULD give out addresses of another account for messaging instead. If they do fetch them, they SHOULD tell the user that the holder of the key can read and delete the account’s messages and send messages in its Conversations.
Any address with an Orchard Receiver is already a public encryption key, so first contact needs nothing new. The cost is the power it gives incoming viewing key holders.
Why derive the mailbox instead of advertising it?

Advertising it would need a ZIP 316 Metadata Item, lengthen addresses, and allow one mailbox to be put in two addresses, linking them. Derivation gives every diversified address its own mailbox. In exchange, senders cannot tell whether a recipient reads messages, wallets have to agree on a Server List, and fetching has to be authorized by a key the wallet already has.
Why is a Mailbox ID a pair of points?

A Contact Mailbox gives its server a record of everything sent to an address. Pairwise Mailboxes move an ongoing exchange to identifiers that change weekly, and they give the recipient a way to answer without the sender disclosing an address. Shorter epochs would leak less but cost a returning wallet one fetch per missed epoch and Conversation.
Why is there no Delete request?
Deleting on the next fetch puts a random delay between reading an Envelope and its disappearance, which the sender in a Conversation can observe.

A party that stores messages for a wallet’s address and also sees the wallet’s IP address, as a Nym gateway named in an address would, can link the two. Here the server that stores Envelopes never sees an IP address, and the entry point that sees one never learns a Mailbox ID. It also means wallets on different networks can exchange messages, and the protocol outlives any one network.
